quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

Mode: **create** — first plan for q_001, "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?"

**Tree survey facts bearing on the question:**
- I1 Patrick Flynn: birth ~1845, Ireland (sourced from 1850 census S1); death 1908-03-12, Schuylkill County, PA (death cert S3)
- I2 Thomas Flynn: birth ~1818, Ireland (no source attached); no death fact in tree

- S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records) cataloged as tree source; zero assertions from it extracted for q_001
- Patrick's mother: completely unidentified; no female Flynn in the tree
- Patrick was born in Ireland, so no Pennsylvania baptism exists for him

---

**Plan pl_002 — 10 items:**

| Seq | Item | Record Type | Place / Date | Repository | Notes |
|-----|------|-------------|--------------|------------|-------|
| 1 | pli_004 | Census | Schuylkill Co., PA — 1860 | FamilySearch | S2 is in tree but no parentage assertions extracted; Patrick (~15) still in Thomas's household, naming the wife/mother |
| 2 | pli_005 | Census | Schuylkill Co., PA — 1870 | FamilySearch | Thomas (~52) likely still head; 1870 returns each person's birthplace |
| 3 | pli_006 | Census | Schuylkill Co., PA — 1880 | FamilySearch | First census to name relationship to head explicitly; Thomas (~62) or Patrick (~35) in own household both carry clues |
| 4 | pli_007 | Census | Schuylkill Co., PA — 1900 | FamilySearch | Patrick (~55) likely head eight years before death; 1900 asks father's and mother's birthplace |
| 5 | pli_008 | Probate | Schuylkill Co., PA — 1855–1895 | FamilySearch | Thomas's will naming Patrick as son is direct evidence; widow named as legatee identifies the mother. S4 in tree, no assertions extracted |
| 6 | pli_009 | Church | Schuylkill Co., PA — 1840–1855 | FamilySearch | Thomas & wife's marriage: confirms the couple, supplies the wife's maiden name. Name-searchable SYNTH-PA-CHURCH |
| 7 | pli_010 | Church (fallback for pli_009) | Schuylkill Co., PA — 1840–1855 | FamilySearch | Browse image group 007936751 (bilingual en/de, browse-only) if name-search yields nothing |
| 8 | pli_011 | Church | Schuylkill Co., PA — 1845–1870 | FamilySearch | Siblings' baptisms born in PA after emigration; each entry records Thomas and wife as parents, naming the mother |
| 9 | pli_012 | Naturalization | Schuylkill Co., PA — 1849–1870 | FamilySearch | Thomas's declaration may name his Irish home parish — a lead for Irish baptism records if PA evidence is insufficient |
| 10 | pli_013 | Land / FAN | Schuylkill Co., PA — 1845–1890 | FamilySearch | Deed boundary recitals name adjoining landowners; frequently fellow Irish immigrants who are kinsmen or witnesses |

---

**Narrative rationale**

Because Patrick was born in Ireland around 1845 and the family had settled in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania by the 1850 census, the most direct route to identifying his mother is the household she shared with Thomas Flynn in the decades following immigration. The plan begins with the 1860, 1870, and 1880 federal census records — all fully name-searchable — which would show Thomas Flynn's complete family, with his wife named alongside him; the 1880 census is especially useful because it was the first to record each person's exact relationship to the head of household. A fourth census search covers 1900, by which time Patrick himself was head of household and the census asked for each person's parents' birthplaces.

After the census searches, the plan turns to Thomas Flynn's will or estate papers filed in Schuylkill County — a will naming Patrick as a son is the most direct evidence of fatherhood available, and any widow named as heir would identify the mother in a single document. The church records searches look first for Thomas and his wife's marriage (which would give the mother's maiden name), with a browse of the bilingual image-only register as a fallback, then for baptisms of younger siblings born in Pennsylvania after arrival. Finally, Thomas Flynn's naturalization papers and Schuylkill County deed records round out the plan.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Children who predeceased Thomas would not be listed, so this source complements rather than replaces the census evidence. Collection 1992421 (loc_001) covers Ohio probate records from 1789–1996. Each child's own 1880 household can also be checked for unmarried siblings still at home.

Children of Thomas and Sarah would marry and appear in Ohio county marriage records. Searching for brides and grooms surnamed Hale in Greene County from roughly 1854 (when Mary, born ~1836, would reach marriageable age) through 1900 may reveal previously unidentified children. A daughter's record would carry the Hale maiden name; a record naming her father as Thomas confirms parentage. The locality entry (loc_001) notes collection 1614804 covers Ohio county marriages 1789–2016. The date range extends past 1868 because children born in the late 1840s and 1850s — if any exist — would marry after Thomas's death.

Ohio civil birth registration did not begin until 1867, and compliance was poor for years afterward. A search for Hale baptisms in Greene County churches covering the period when Thomas and Sarah were raising their family may identify children who died in infancy or early childhood and are thus absent from every census. This covers the birth record type required for an enumerative question.

Ohio civil death registration began in 1867. Early death records may name parents, enabling identification of a child of Thomas and Sarah who died after that date. Cemetery and burial records (including FindAGrave transcriptions for Greene County) may show Hale family plots with multiple children buried together — including those who died young and never appeared in a household census. Thomas Hale's 1868 obituary in a Greene County newspaper — the Xenia Gazette or a similar local paper — may list his surviving children by name, providing a direct enumeration of those alive at his death. This is also a FAN-cluster source: community members mentioned in connection with the Hale family may be unidentified children or children-in-law who have changed surnames. After Thomas's 1868 death, an administrator's sale or partition of his real estate would name each heir receiving a share. Adjoining landowners named in boundary descriptions are also FAN-cluster names and may be relatives or unidentified children who settled nearby. quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

The marriage record would supply the mother's maiden name — absent from both census records and the 1908 death certificate — and by its date relative to Patrick's ~1845 birth corroborates Thomas as father. This record does not by itself establish that Patrick is their child; that link rests on the census co-residence evidence already established. Search under both Flynn and Flinn.

Required FAN item for this parentage question. The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable. items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

entry.rationale: Thomas Flynn (born Ireland ca. 1818, in Schuylkill County by 1850) is Patrick's only proposed father — named by a secondary informant (son-in-law) on the death certificate. A will or letters of administration naming Patrick Flynn as an heir would be direct evidence of the parent-child relationship. The loc_001 locality guide confirms Schuylkill County probate records (Register of Wills) are available from 1811 and are a primary parentage source naming heirs. 'Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994' (collection 1999196) is browse-only (personCount 0); the Schuylkill County volume (image group 007936749) covers 1851-1930 and encompasses Thomas's estimated death window (ca. 1865-1910, based on his ca. 1818 birth). Also search Thomas Flynn's wife's probate: Patrick's mother's will or administration may independently name him. Search under 'Flynn,' 'Flinn,' and 'Flin.'

The 1880 U.S. census was the first to record each person's relationship to the household head — unlike the 1850 and 1860 censuses already searched, which required researcher inference from household position. Thomas Flynn (ca. 1818) would be ca. 62 in 1880; if Patrick (ca. 35) or any sibling appears in Thomas's household as 'son,' that entry is direct evidence of parentage, qualitatively stronger than the existing indirect co-residence assertions. The 1880 U.S. Federal Census on FamilySearch is name-searchable. The 1880 search also serves a FAN purpose: any other children listed as 'son' or 'daughter' under Thomas reveal siblings whose later records (marriage, death) can be searched independently.

Patrick Flynn's own marriage record would name his parents, providing direct evidence of his father. Patrick (ca. 1845) likely married ca. 1865-1885: his son-in-law James Brown was the informant on the 1908 death certificate, meaning Patrick's daughter was adult by 1908 and was likely born ca. 1875-1885, placing Patrick's marriage ca. 1865-1880. 'Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950' (collection 1571957) is name-searchable and covers the estimated window. 'Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950' (collection 1921317) is name-searchable and covers the later end. Search both collections under 'Flynn,' 'Flinn,' and 'Flin.' quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.question: Did Michael Sheahan move to Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania around 1882 for anthracite coal-mining work, as family tradition holds?
items.rationale: log_001 places Michael as a farmer in a different county in 1870; log_002 places him in Schuylkill County by 1882 with occupation 'miner'. The occupation and location both changed between these two points, consistent with a work-driven relocation to the anthracite coal region, but nothing yet directly documents the move itself or its cause -- no land purchase, employment record, or correspondence has been found for Michael himself. No plan has yet been written for this question.

entry.rationale: The 1880 US census is the critical anchor for the move. The tree records Michael's Schuylkill County residence only from 1882; the 1880 census (collection 1417683, name-searchable) taken just two years earlier will show whether Michael was already in Schuylkill County (pushing the move before 1882) or still farming elsewhere in Pennsylvania (narrowing the move to 1880-1882). Brother Patrick Sheahan (I2) purchased land in Schuylkill County in 1875 (S1), so finding Michael in the same household or township in 1880 would directly support chain migration as the mechanism. Search under Sheahan and variant spellings Sheehan, Shihan.

The tree already records Michael's 1870 residence as 'Pennsylvania, United States'; the question rationale specifies he was a farmer in a different (non-Schuylkill) county that year. The 1870 US census (collection 1438024, name-searchable) will identify which county Michael and potentially Patrick Sheahan occupied before the Schuylkill move, corroborate the farmer occupation, and establish the geographic starting point of the migration. If Patrick Sheahan also appears here in the same non-Schuylkill county in 1870 but is in Schuylkill County by 1875 (per S1), the two censuses together establish the sequence of the brothers' separate moves. Include Sheehan, Shihan as spelling variants.

The 1900 US census (collection 1325221, name-searchable) is the first federal census to record immigration year and years in the US for foreign-born persons, as well as years married. Michael is expected in Schuylkill County by 1900 as a miner. His birthplace, immigration year (if foreign-born), and duration in the US situate the 1882 move within his life arc and may point to an origin community already present in the anthracite coal region — which would explain why Schuylkill County specifically was the destination. Finding him alongside Patrick Sheahan in 1900 would further confirm the family-network explanation for the move.

Roman Catholic parishes in Schuylkill County fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia (archdiocese from 1875); sacramental registers are held at the parish level (loc_001). The 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' collection on FamilySearch is name-searchable (personCount above 0). Michael's first appearance in a Schuylkill parish register documents when he arrived in the county — before or after 1882 — and a sacramental record in the same parish as Patrick Sheahan (I2) would directly support chain migration. Also search for Patrick Sheahan here to establish his earliest parish registration, which anchors when his own Schuylkill residency began. Include Sheehan and Shihan variants. A separate browse-only church-records volume (image group 007936751, 1842-1895, English and German) covers earlier decades if the indexed collection gaps arise.

FAN item — brother Patrick Sheahan (I2). Patrick purchased land in Schuylkill County in 1875 (S1, Deed Book 42 p. 118), establishing himself there 7 years before Michael's documented 1882 arrival. Searching the 1870 and 1880 censuses specifically for Patrick Sheahan will reveal where he lived in 1870 (the family's origin county, compared against Michael's 1870 location) and confirm his Schuylkill County presence in 1880. If Patrick and Michael shared a county in 1870 and Patrick was already in Schuylkill by 1875-1880, the sequential movement strongly supports family-network chain migration rather than independent job-seeking as the cause. This FAN search targets evidence about Michael's motivation for the move, not Patrick's own genealogy.

Image group 007936750 (Schuylkill County Naturalization Records, 1849-1915) is a browse-only image group (personCount 0) on FamilySearch; loc_001 notes these films are browse-only for the anthracite region. If Michael Sheahan was foreign-born, his Declaration of Intention (First Papers) and Petition for Naturalization filed in Schuylkill County would state his country of origin, prior US residence, occupation, and how long he had lived in the county — direct evidence of when he relocated to Schuylkill County and from where. Browse images concentrated in the 1882-1895 window, where a newly arrived laborer would most likely have filed his first papers.

Pennsylvania statewide civil death registration began in 1906 (loc_001); if Michael Sheahan died after that year, his death certificate will state birthplace, parents' names, length of Pennsylvania residence, and the informant — all useful for tracing his origin and confirming the 1882 move timeline. The 'Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968' collection (collection 2255317) is name-searchable. A birthplace outside Pennsylvania would establish him as an immigrant who arrived at or before 1882; a stated origin in another Pennsylvania county would corroborate the farmer-to-miner transition the 1870-1882 records imply. Search Sheahan, Sheehan, Shihan.

entry.repository: Pennsylvania State Archives / Schuylkill County Historical Society
entry.rationale: Mine employment records — colliery payrolls, anthracite operators' records, and annual Pennsylvania Bureau of Mines inspector reports — would directly document which mine or colliery Michael Sheahan worked for and when he first appeared on the employment rolls, the closest available evidence to a documented reason for the move. These records are not digitized and are not in any indexed FamilySearch or Ancestry collection. The Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) and the Schuylkill County Historical Society (Pottsville) hold selected colliery records and Bureau of Mines materials for this region. This item follows the FamilySearch searches so that any employer name, mine name, or company appearing in an indexed record can be used to target the correct colliery's employment file. An on-site or written inquiry to these repositories is required.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

entry.rationale: The 1880 census was the first federal census to record each person's relationship to the head of household. If Patrick (~35) remains in Thomas Flynn's household, the relationship column may directly state 'son' — the first direct census statement of the parent-child relationship and the single item most likely to advance the conclusion from 'probable' to 'proved.' Even if Patrick heads his own household, the record reveals his wife's name, children, and any widowed mother living with them, identifying the unknown mother. Collection 'United States Census, 1880' (1417683) is name-searchable. Prior plan pl_002 completed the 1860 census and death certificate; this plan targets the three unsearched census years and Thomas Flynn's probate identified as gaps in ps_001.

Patrick (~25) and Thomas (~52) in 1870; the 1870 census has no relationship column, but Patrick's continued presence in or near Thomas Flynn's household corroborates the parent-child relationship established indirectly in 1850 and 1860. If Thomas died before 1870, Patrick's own household may show a widowed mother living with him — potentially identifying the unknown mother. Collection 'United States Census, 1870' (1438024) is name-searchable.

Patrick (~55) in 1900 confirms continued Schuylkill County residence and reveals household composition: wife, children, and possibly a widowed mother or in-laws. The 1900 census asks for years married, number of children born, and number living — useful for understanding family structure and generating FAN leads. James Brown (son-in-law, death-cert informant) may appear as a household member or neighbor, providing additional context. Collection 'United States Census, 1900' (1325221) is name-searchable.

Thomas Flynn (born ~1818) last appeared in the 1860 census at approximately age 42; his death date is unknown. A will or estate administration naming Patrick as a son would be direct evidence of parentage — the record most likely to definitively prove the relationship. Per loc_001, probate records are held by the Schuylkill County Register of Wills, available from 1811. Collection 'Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994' (1999196) is browse-only (personCount 0); image group 007936749 covers 1851-1930 and is also browse-only (personCount 0). The tree already holds source description S4 'Schuylkill County Probate Records' with no assertions extracted, confirming this record type was identified but not yet searched. Date range set to 1861–1920, covering Thomas's plausible lifespan from the year following his last census appearance through approximately age 102 — the outer bound of the image group.

Patrick's mother has not been named in any record found so far. For a parentage conclusion that identifies both parents, the parents' marriage record is required: it names the wife (Patrick's mother), establishes Thomas and his wife as a couple, and by its date relative to Patrick's ~1845 birth corroborates Thomas as father. Per loc_001, Roman Catholic parishes in Schuylkill County fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia; sacramental registers are held at the parish or diocese level. Thomas (~born 1818) likely married in his twenties, so a Schuylkill marriage circa 1840-1848 is plausible if he emigrated before Patrick's birth. Collection 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable (personCount 982415), covering 1708-1985. Search Flynn, Flyn, and Flinn. Note: if Thomas married in Ireland before emigrating, this collection will not hold the record.

Fallback for pli_010 (Thomas Flynn marriage, name-searchable church records). If the indexed collection returns no marriage for Thomas Flynn under any spelling variant, browse image group 007936751 (Church Records 1842-1895, Schuylkill County, browse-only, personCount 0) image by image. Per loc_001, some coal-region church films are browse-only; the parish register the indexed collection draws from may be incomplete or have variant spellings that eluded indexing.

FAN item required for a parentage question. If Thomas and his wife had children born in Schuylkill County after emigrating, those children's baptism entries would directly name both parents — providing corroborating evidence for Patrick's parentage and identifying the mother's maiden name. The 1850 Thomas Flynn household may include other children not named in extracted assertions; this search targets potential siblings born ca. 1845-1865. Collection 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable (personCount 982415); search for baptisms with parent name Thomas Flynn (and variants Flyn, Flinn). Each sibling's baptism entry that names both parents would constitute independent corroboration of the parentage line.

Patrick had at least one daughter (James Brown is named as son-in-law on the 1908 death certificate). Pennsylvania county marriage records often name the groom's father and place of origin. Finding Patrick's marriage would yield (a) a secondary statement of his father's name if listed, (b) his wife's identity and family (FAN), and (c) a date and church for further research. The marriage also fills the high-severity timeline gap (1860-1908, expected event 'marriage'). Date range sized to the image group rather than cut at Patrick's death: the image group runs through 1910 but Patrick died 1908, so the upper bound is effectively 1908.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

**Plan pl_002 written and validated.**

**Mode:** Create — first research plan for q_001, "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?"

**Tree facts bearing on the question:**
- Patrick Flynn (I1): Birth ~1845 in Ireland (from 1850 census); Death 1908-03-12 Schuylkill County, PA (death cert S3, cert no. 4521)
- Thomas Flynn (I2): Birth ~1818 Ireland; no death date or place recorded; listed as Patrick's parent via relationship R1
- R1 (Thomas→Patrick): cited on S1 (1850 census), S2 (1860 census), S3 (death cert) — all quality 2, indirect; Thomas's fatherhood is a strong candidate, not yet proved
- S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records) is in the tree as a source description but no assertions from it
- No mother appears anywhere in the tree

---

**Plan pl_002 — 9 items in execution order:**

- **pli_004** | vital_record | Schuylkill County, PA | FamilySearch | 1908 — Patrick's 1908 death cert (cert no. 4521); PA death certs from 1906 onward include father's name and mother's maiden name; highest-yield source for both parents
- **pli_005** | census | Schuylkill County, PA | FamilySearch | 1860 — S2 cited on the Thomas–Patrick relationship but no q_001 assertions extracted; Patrick (~age 15) very likely still in Thomas's household
- **pli_006** | census | Schuylkill County, PA | FamilySearch | 1880 — first census to explicitly record relationship to head of household; also asks for parents' birthplaces
- **pli_007** | census | Schuylkill County, PA | FamilySearch | 1900 — asks each person for their father's and mother's birthplace; Patrick (~age 55) alive for this enumeration
- **pli_008** | probate | Schuylkill County, PA | FamilySearch | 1851–1930 — S4 is in the tree as a source description but not yet searched; Thomas's will would name heirs (Patrick as son = direct parentage evidence) and may name the surviving spouse
- **pli_009** | church | Schuylkill County, PA | FamilySearch | 1840–1858 — parents' marriage record confirms the couple as a unit and supplies the mother's maiden name
- **pli_010** | church | Schuylkill County, PA | FamilySearch | 1845–1855 — a baptism record names both parents directly; conditional or arrival baptism in a PA Catholic parish is plausible
- **pli_011** | census (FAN cluster) | Schuylkill County, PA | FamilySearch | 1850–1870 — Irish immigrants in the anthracite region settled in townland clusters; a Flynn neighbor who is a sibling of Thomas leads to collateral records naming Thomas's wife
- **pli_012** | naturalization | Schuylkill County, PA | FamilySearch | 1849–1915 — naturalization petitions typically include the petitioner's exact town, parish, and county in Ireland; Thomas's petition likely filed 1845–1870

**Total scope:** 9 searches, all on FamilySearch, covering vital records, three census years, probate, two church record types, a FAN-cluster census review, and naturalization.

---

**Summary of strategy:** The plan opens with Patrick's 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate, which by law from 1906 onward included specific lines for the father's name and mother's maiden name — that single document may answer the question outright. It then works through three federal census years (1860, 1880, and 1900), Thomas Flynn's probate records, two church record searches (marriage and baptism), a FAN-cluster review of neighboring households, and Thomas's naturalization petition — which would likely name his exact Irish parish of origin, opening the door to Irish records if American sources do not resolve the question.

**Next step:** Search for Patrick Flynn's 1908 death certificate on FamilySearch (pli_004), then proceed through the census records.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

entry.rationale: Patrick Flynn's 1908 death certificate (project source S3, cert no. 4521) is already cited in the tree for his Death fact, but no parentage assertions have been extracted from it for q_001. Pennsylvania statewide civil registration began in 1906 (loc_001), so this certificate was issued contemporaneously and includes dedicated lines for the father's name and the mother's maiden name filled in by the informant. This is the single highest-yield step for identifying Patrick's parents. The 1908 death cert is browse-only (personCount 0) in the Pennsylvania Death Certificates collection — retrieve the full image and extract the informant's statement of both parents' names.

The 1860 U.S. Census is already cited on the Thomas-Patrick parentage relationship in the project tree (S2), but no parentage assertions for q_001 have been extracted from it. Patrick (born ~1845) would be approximately 15 in 1860 and very likely still in Thomas Flynn's household. Co-enumeration in 1860 provides a second data point beyond the 1850 census (a_004) and strengthens the inference that Thomas is Patrick's father. The 1860 census did not explicitly record relationships to the head of household, but shared dwelling confirms the family unit. Search FamilySearch for Flynn (also try Flyn, Flin) in Schuylkill County.

The 1880 U.S. Census is the first federal census to explicitly record each person's relationship to the head of household. Patrick (born ~1845, age ~35 in 1880) may still be in Thomas Flynn's household or enumerated on his own. If Thomas (born ~1818) is alive, the 1880 census would record 'Father' or 'Son' as the relationship — direct evidence of parentage. The 1880 census also asks for the birthplace of each person's father and mother, which could confirm Irish origins and corroborate Thomas's role. Variant spellings: Flynn, Flyn, Flin.

The 1900 U.S. Census asks each person for the birthplace of their father and mother — the most directly useful census column for tracing Irish parentage. Patrick (born ~1845) would be approximately 55 in 1900 and is known to have died 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County (S3), confirming he was alive for this enumeration. His recorded 'Father's birthplace' and 'Mother's birthplace' entries could pinpoint the Irish county or province of his parents' origins. Variant spellings: Flynn, Flyn, Flin.

Probate records are a primary source for parentage because a will names the testator's heirs — typically children by name — and often names the surviving spouse. S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records) is already a source description in the project tree, indicating this source was previously identified, but no assertions have been made from it for q_001. Thomas Flynn (born ~1818) could have died anywhere from roughly 1860 to 1920; the applicable image group 007936749 covers Schuylkill County probate 1851-1930 and is browse-only (personCount 0). A will naming Patrick Flynn as Thomas's son would be direct parentage evidence; a named spouse or co-heir would identify Patrick's mother. Per loc_001, probate records are held by the Schuylkill County Register of Wills, available from 1811. The Pennsylvania Probate Records collection 1683-1994 (1999196) is also browse-only (personCount 0) — browse both. Thomas's lifespan (born ~1818) sets the date window's bounds.

The parents' marriage record is a required search for a parentage question: it confirms Thomas and his wife married as a couple, supplies the mother's maiden name (which census and death records usually omit), and by its date relative to Patrick's birth ~1845, corroborates Thomas as Patrick's father beyond census co-enumeration alone. The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable (personCount 982,415) and spans 1708-1985, covering the likely marriage period. Search for Thomas Flynn with variant spellings (Flynn, Flyn, Flin). Per loc_001, Roman Catholic parishes in Schuylkill County were under the Diocese of Philadelphia (archdiocese 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown in 1961. Note the limit: this marriage record proves the couple wed but does not by itself establish Patrick as their child — that link requires a separate record placing Patrick with them (baptism, census household, or probate).

A baptism record is direct evidence of parentage, naming both parents at the time of the event. Patrick was born ~1845 in Ireland (F1, tree), but the family was already in Schuylkill County by the 1850 census (age 5). If the family emigrated in 1845-1850, a Catholic parish in Schuylkill County may have baptized Patrick upon arrival or recorded a conditional baptism. His birth parish in Ireland is unknown (the unknown being sought), so his PA church records are the first avenue. The SYNTH-PA-CHURCH collection is name-searchable (personCount 982,415). Per loc_001, RC parishes were under the Diocese of Philadelphia; sacramental registers are held at the parish and diocese. If the indexed search finds nothing, also browse image group 007936751 (Schuylkill County church records, 1842-1895, English/German, browse-only (personCount 0)).

A parentage question requires at least one FAN-directed search (BCG Standard 14). Irish immigrants in the Schuylkill County anthracite region frequently settled in clusters from the same townland or parish. Reviewing the neighboring households in the 1850 enumeration (Thomas at dwelling 84, family 91, per a_003) and the 1860 and 1870 enumerations may reveal individuals with the Flynn surname (possible siblings or cousins of Thomas) or Irish immigrants who appear later in the same church registers, naturalization records, or probate proceedings. A neighbor who is a likely sibling of Thomas could lead to collateral records naming Thomas's parents and wife. This item targets what the neighbors' records reveal about Thomas and Patrick, not the neighbors' own genealogy.

Naturalization petitions from the 1850s-1900s typically include the petitioner's exact place of birth (town, parish, county in Ireland). Knowing the origin parish for Thomas Flynn (born ~1818, Ireland) or for Patrick (born ~1845, Ireland) would enable targeted searching of Irish baptism and marriage registers, greatly expanding the evidence base for identifying Patrick's parents. Image group 007936750 covers Schuylkill County naturalization records 1849-1915 and is browse-only (personCount 0). Thomas likely naturalized between 1845 and 1870; Patrick may have naturalized after reaching majority. Thomas's lifespan and the known emigration window (pre-1850) set the practical date window for Thomas's petition.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.

Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.
